soil-fert-260.title: Composting in pits and closed vessels
soil-fert-260.text: Not every compost pile sits in the open. Small farmers in developing countries, especially in dry and hot climates, dig compost pits. A layer of soil over the top keeps animals out and holds moisture in. Home composters often choose closed vessels instead. A vessel makes turning easier, gives better control of temperature and moisture, and keeps rodents away. At commercial scale, though, vessels are generally not economical.

soil-fert-240.title: Two kinds of crop-livestock farm
soil-fert-240.text: Some farms grow all or nearly all of their animal feed, and they come in two general types. One mainly sells animal products and matches animal numbers to the land's carrying capacity: grass-fed beef, pastured hogs, or a dairy growing its own grain and forage. The other is the diversified farm, which raises all its feed but sells a range of crops and animal products. Multiple products protect against seasonal failure and price swings. On both, crops feed animals and {{ref:soil-fert-023}} returns to the soil, a continuous supply of organic materials. Perennial forages cut erosion and keep or raise soil organic matter.

soil-fert-242.title: Solid, semi-solid or liquid: how dairy manure is handled
soil-fert-242.text: On a dairy farm, the barn often decides how {{ref:soil-fert-023}} is handled. Manure with bedding at around 20% dry matter or more is spread as a solid. Liquid manure from free-stall barns is 2-12% dry matter, and the 12-20% range is semi-solid, as with pasture cow manure. {{ref:soil-fert-029}} stabilizes nutrients, though considerable ammonium is lost, and leaves less, more pleasant material to spread. Separating liquid from solids lets the solids compost without added material and eases transport. Compost barns stir the bedded pack twice daily to 8-10 inches and clear it in spring or fall. Vermicomposting uses worms to turn dairy manure into castings. Industrial hog farms use slatted floors over pits and hold liquid manure in ponds for spring and fall spreading, while small hoop-house hog systems use bedding.

soil-fert-269.title: Grading a nitrogen rate after harvest
soil-fert-269.text: Was last season's nitrogen rate too low, about right or too high? Farmers can find out after harvest. One way is to plant field strips at different N rates and compare yields. Another is to sample soil nitrate after harvest, a 'report card' assessment of residual available N. The lower stalk nitrate test also shows whether corn N rates were right, too low or too high. Each answer guides rates in the following years.

soil-fert-267.title: Maximum return to nitrogen for corn
soil-fert-267.text: One way to set a corn nitrogen rate is to pick a single number: the rate with the largest average net return over many field trials. This is the maximum return to nitrogen. It draws on extensive trials, model fitting and economics, so recommendations vary with grain and fertilizer prices. The strength is also the weakness. Because it generalizes over large areas and many seasons, it ignores soil and weather effects. For an individual field, it is imprecise.

soil-fert-264.title: How much nitrogen compost really supplies
soil-fert-264.text: The richer an amendment is in nitrogen, the larger the share of that nitrogen plants can use. Compost or another organic amendment with about 2 percent N or less, a high C:N, supplies little to no available N. At about 5 percent N, roughly 40 percent is available. At 10-15 percent N, 70 percent or more is. Fertilizer should supplement what soil organic matter, manure, compost and rotation or cover crops already supply. Organic farmers try to meet all demands from these sources.

soil-fert-268.title: The pre-sidedress nitrate test
soil-fert-268.text: In late spring, a soil sample can say whether a corn field needs more nitrogen. The pre-sidedress nitrate test measures nitrate in the top 0-12 inches and guides sidedress or topdress nitrogen. It implicitly captures early-season weather and is especially good at identifying sites that need no more N fertilizer. The catch is timing. It needs special sampling in a short late-spring window and is sensitive to timing and early-spring mineralization. In the US Midwest it is called the late spring nitrate test. It was the first approach to address dynamic N processes, giving more precise recommendations and cutting unnecessary N applications.

soil-fert-257.title: Dung patches: uneven fertility on pasture
soil-fert-257.text: A grazing animal fertilizes in spots. Animals on pasture drop excrement on the surface, making small concentrated nutrient spots between which the soil is poorer. Some ammonium and urea is lost to the air as the pies dry. Dense vegetation keeps runoff low and nitrogen leaching less of a concern. Yet because the patches are unevenly spread, nitrate leaching can still occur on intensively managed, fertilized dairy pasture.

soil-fert-256.title: When a herd outgrows its land
soil-fert-256.text: Feed bought from off the farm carries nutrients with it, and they stay behind as manure. A farm whose herd exceeds its land base therefore accumulates them. Integrated crop-livestock farms that grow most of their feed keep nutrient imports and exports near balance. Farms with animal numbers beyond their land's feed output risk nutrient buildup and groundwater and surface water pollution. The options are sharing manure with neighbours, composting and selling it, or drying it to ease transport.

soil-fert-255.title: The Phosphorus Index: scoring the risk of runoff
soil-fert-255.text: Where will phosphorus leave a field and reach a stream? The Phosphorus Index is a tool for assessing that risk. It combines source factors, such as soil test P, total soil P and the rate, method and timing of P application. It also counts transport factors: sediment delivery, field position in the watershed, conservation practices, precipitation, runoff and tile drainage. A nutrient planner uses it to rate P movement risk as low, medium or high and to suggest mitigation.

soil-fert-246.title: Three forms of nitrogen in manure
soil-fert-246.text: Manure nitrogen is not one thing. It occurs as ammonium, as urea, which is soluble and quickly converted to ammonium, and as solid organic N. Ammonium and urea are readily available to crops, but they are lost as ammonia gas when left on a drying surface, with significant losses within hours (see {{ref:soil-fert-084}}). Mixes differ by animal. Some manures have half to three-quarters of N in readily available form, others 20% or less. Cattle manure is fairly balanced between available and organic N, while swine manure N is mostly ammonium or urea. Reports give ammonium and total N, the difference being mostly organic N. This is the nitrogen in {{ref:soil-fert-023}} that behaves most differently from one load to the next.

soil-fert-249.title: How much manure to spread
soil-fert-249.text:
Farmers usually spread manure at a rate judged to supply the current crop's nitrogen, drawing on the forms described in {{ref:soil-fert-246}}. Common dairy rates are 10-30 tons solid or 4,000-11,000 gallons liquid per acre, supplying about 50-150 pounds available N. Small grains need 10-15 tons, corn 20-30 tons. Higher rates may build organic matter but risk nitrate buildup in leafy crops, nitrate leaching, salt damage and excess soil phosphorus. Where soil P is far above optimum, apply by crop P need and export part of the manure.

Manure on legumes is discouraged, because the legume then fixes less N, though it can suit intensive animal farms with excess N. Manure P and K availability resembles fertilizer. Twenty tons of dairy manure give about 30-50 pounds phosphate and 180-200 pounds potash.

soil-fert-272.title: Why corn wastes so much nitrogen
soil-fert-272.text: Corn turns each extra pound of absorbed nitrogen into more yield than most crops. Even so, corn systems typically use fertilizer N at under 50 percent efficiency. Leaching, denitrification and runoff losses are much higher for corn than for soybeans or wheat, and especially than alfalfa and grass. The causes are growth cycle, rates, timing and rooting depth. Many farmers also add 'insurance' N for wet years, though they may need it only about one season in four.

soil-fert-271.title: Counting the nitrogen last year's crop left behind
soil-fert-271.text:
Before buying nitrogen, subtract what the field already holds. Fertilizer decisions should deduct the N supplied by manure, decomposing sods and legume or cover crops. Example credits, in pounds per acre: corn 0; soybeans 0-40; 2-year clover 70; 3-year alfalfa 70 (20-60% legume) or 120 (>60%); crimson clover, winter peas and excellent hairy vetch 110.

These credits are the N available to the crop, not the total in the residue. Sandy soils get less, and cover crop growth stage and amount matter strongly. High-yielding legume covers such as hairy vetch and crimson clover can supply most or all of the N for the next crop. Many labs, however, do not ask about cover crops.

soil-fert-273.title: The risk of broadcasting fertilizer on no-till
soil-fert-273.text: Broadcast fertilizer is fast: it covers 500-800 acres in eight hours, against about 200 for injection. In no-till, the speed has a cost in nitrogen and phosphorus losses. After intense storms, surface urea can wash into wormholes and deep into the subsoil, so N should not be broadcast and left on the surface. Residue urease speeds urea conversion to ammonia gas. Phosphorus builds up on no-till surfaces, and dissolved P in runoff is often higher than from tilled soil. P should therefore be applied below the surface.

soil-fert-259.title: Curing: the last stage of compost
soil-fert-259.text: Hot composting ends with a quiet phase of one to three months called curing, in which the pile cools and finishes its decomposition. It starts once temperatures drop to about 105 degrees F and no longer rebound after turning. A pile that reheats is not finished, and the Solvita test measures CO2 loss to judge maturity. Curing further breaks down resistant chemicals and large particles, brings pH toward neutral, converts ammonium to nitrate, leaches soluble salts and lets common soil organisms colonize. Moisture should stay at or below about 50 percent. The early curing processes are thought to give compost some of its disease-suppressing quality.

soil-fert-244.title: Turning manure into biogas
soil-fert-244.text: On large livestock farms, anaerobic digesters process manure to make biogas, mostly methane. The gas fuels on-farm heat and electricity or off-farm vehicles, and digesters can cut greenhouse gas emissions, odors and pathogens. They are a major capital investment, though, and may not pay without subsidies, energy, carbon credits, tipping fees and coproducts. Nor do they solve the nutrient problem. They separate liquid and solids but generally do not change total nutrient content, so excess nutrients and runoff remain. The input is still {{ref:soil-fert-023}}, only processed.

soil-fert-247.title: Why manures differ in what they add to organic matter
soil-fert-247.text:
Equal amounts of different manures do not affect {{ref:soil-found-045}} equally. The difference is how much solid is returned. Dairy and beef manures hold undigested forage and bedding rich in lignin, so they influence organic matter far more than unbedded poultry or swine manure. Sand bedding and separating solids return less organic material to fields, whereas a bedded pack is high in solids.

With corn silage under conventional tillage, 20 to 30 tons of solid dairy manure per acre yearly maintain organic matter; less is needed if more residue returns. The arithmetic is humbling. Twenty tons of manure holds about 5,200 pounds of solids. Mixed into the top 6 inches, it would raise organic matter about 0.3%, but if 75% decomposes the net gain is 0.065%. Still, the effect shows in the field: New York samples of 300 fields showed dairy-crop fields receiving manure averaged 0.5% higher organic matter than cash grain fields.

soil-fert-248.title: What years of manure do to a soil
soil-fert-248.text:
Manure changes a soil in biological, chemical and physical ways. An 11-year Vermont experiment grew continuous corn silage, a monoculture with low residue return. Twenty tons of dairy manure yearly kept organic matter and CEC levels, and the pH stayed close to the original, offsetting that low return. Dairy and poultry manures have a liming effect and counteract acidification.

The physical changes were as clear. Manured plots were better aggregated and less dense. Organic matter was 5.2% originally, 4.3% unmanured and 5.2% at 30 tons, with pore space 44% versus 47%. Liquid manure supplying the same N would not have raised organic matter, CEC and pore space nearly as much, a link back to {{ref:soil-fert-247}}.

soil-fert-243.title: What manure loses while it waits
soil-fert-243.text: Storing manure lets farmers apply it at the best time for the crop, cutting runoff, leaching and gaseous losses. But storage itself loses nutrients. In one study, dairy manure in uncovered piles lost over a year 3% of solids, 10% of nitrogen, 3% of phosphorus and 20% of potassium. Covered piles and bottom-loading liquid systems with a surface crust conserve nutrients better. Poultry manure may lose 50% of its nitrogen as ammonia unless protected. Potassium is soluble and sits mostly in the liquid portion, so a stack that lets water drain may lose much of it. All of this concerns {{ref:soil-fert-023}} kept waiting.
